meta.title: Kvist — a supervised coding agent for one workspace
meta.description: Kvist is a terminal coding agent that works in one project directory. It works through tool calling (JSON fallback for models without it) in a sandbox that masks secrets, blocks .env, and asks before anything dangerous. Python, MIT, open source.
meta.ogAlt: The Kvist wordmark drawn in terminal half-blocks

langbar.text: This page is also in Russian.

hero.h1: One workspace. One gate for every action.
hero.lede: Kvist is a terminal coding agent that works in a single project directory. It works through tool calling — read, edit, run, verify — and feeds the results back before deciding the next step. Models without tool calling fall back to JSON. Every action goes through one executor that can refuse it.
hero.note: Kvist is released, with source available under the MIT license. The recorded run below shows the real interface. Linux and Windows · macOS without guarantees

demo.h2: A real run, not a rehearsal
demo.lede: Screen recordings of Kvist building a small Python project from a single request, in two of its interfaces. Same agent, same core; pick the look you prefer. The video loads only when you press play.

loop.h2: Tool calling, a few changes at a time
loop.lede: A request is routed to a role and executed step by step through tool calling; a model or provider without it falls back to JSON. In one response the model may ask for any number of reads and searches, which run side by side, up to four at a time. Edits and commands are capped at eight per response and run in order, and a failed one stops the rest. The action set is closed — the model cannot invent a new capability mid-run.

items.text: read_file, write_file, replace_in_file, search_code, run_shell, git_diff, fetch_url, delegate_task, refuse, final_answer and eleven more. The list is a Literal in protocol.py, and a test fails the build if the prompts, the parser and the executor drift apart.

coder edits, reader investigates without writing, devops handles services and deployment, chat answers without touching files, universal chats and acts as the request needs and is the default when nothing else fits. Routing tries explicit rules first, then a small model, then keywords — in that order, in English and Russian.

Every result the model can be influenced by — file contents, search hits, shell output, fetched pages — is wrapped in a delimited block, and a forged closing tag inside the payload is defanged before it reaches the prompt.

The model does not report a percentage. Progress is derived from the phase each response is in — inspect, plan, edit, verify — and only moves forward. When the step budget runs out, Kvist asks whether to continue instead of stopping silently.

boundary.lede: The parts that hold are the ones that never read the prompt. A hostile file, a poisoned web page or a confused model all meet the same gates.

items.text: Reading or writing a .env file is blocked on the path check, before the file is opened, and blocked again for shell commands. The refusal names the violation instead of failing quietly.

Under Bubblewrap the sandbox shadows .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .kube and .azure, id_rsa / id_ed25519 / id_ecdsa, .netrc, .npmrc, .git-credentials and every .pem, .key, .p12, .pfx and .crt. Files become /dev/null, directories become empty tmpfs — so a path built at runtime finds nothing either.

items.term: No network from the shell by default
items.text: The sandbox unshares the network namespace unless AGENT_SANDBOX_NET is set to allow. PID, IPC and UTS namespaces are unshared too, host /home and /root are hidden, and the host root is never bound.

items.term: Dangerous commands are approved once each
items.text: git push, git reset, git clean, docker rm, docker prune, systemctl start/stop/enable and package-manager install/remove are per-execution approvals. Project policy can deny more, never less: deny and the built-in hard blocks always win over allow.

What you approve is argv plus the resolved cwd, the role, the policy digest, the sandbox profile, the child environment, the target executable's identity and content, and the attested shebang interpreter. If any of it changes before the spawn, the approval is void.

A child that calls setsid() escapes a process group, so the whole subtree runs in a cgroup v2 scope and is torn down with cgroup.kill on both timeout and completion. Output is drained into fixed-size buffers, so a noisy child cannot grow the parent.

boundary.honest: Kvist is a supervised tool, not a security product. Transitive imports are not individually attested, history-aware tools can surface content that never appears in argv, and a narrow window remains between the final check and the spawn. Read the diff.

recovery.h2: Interrupt it without losing the work
recovery.lede: A run writes down what it is about to do before it does it. That is what makes an interrupted run resumable and a change reversible.

items.text: A checkpoint is written before every externally visible action. Resuming follows the checkpoint into the session it belongs to instead of replaying it into whatever session happens to be open.

items.term: /revert only touches what it can prove
items.text: The journal separates a write it can prove it made from content that merely looks right. Reverting overwrites the first and leaves the second alone. A corrupt journal stops the mutation instead of being read as an empty one.

items.term: Sessions are documents, not a scratch buffer
items.text: /new starts a session; it does not erase the previous one. Each session keeps its own history, checkpoint and style, and the style is stamped at the start so a plan and the steps that follow it come from the same beliefs.

control.lede: Providers, effort and tone are settings, not assumptions baked into the agent.

items.term: Six providers, plus your own endpoint
items.text: OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, OmniRoute and FreeFlow, or any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-compatible endpoint you add from /provider. Streaming and JSON mode are per-provider facts, not one assumption applied to all of them.
fast and smart. A run starts on fast and escalates to smart on a complex task, a parse error, repeated errors or stagnation — unless you pinned a model yourself.
false, low, medium, high, xhigh, max — one /effort command, translated per provider. If a provider rejects the setting, Kvist retries without it and warns you every single time.

Nine for the action loop — minimalist, paranoid, architect, perfectionist, senior-dev and more — and five for chat. One session keeps one style, so the executor cannot quietly disagree with the plan it was handed.

items.term: The project states its own rules
items.text: KVIST.md and KVIST-CHAT.md in the workspace root carry your build commands, layout and conventions into every call. They are workspace content, so they are quoted as data inside bounds that rule out changing the role, the safety rules or the action protocol.
A newline-delimited JSON frontend runs Kvist from another process, with session and journal operations available as one-shot commands. The Electron GUI uses that same protocol and nothing else.

anymodel.h2: One key, many models, lower prices
anymodel.lede: AnyModel is the provider Kvist suggests on a clean machine. One key opens a large catalog, and some features exist only through it.

items.text: AnyModel resells models at prices well below the original providers. Kvist reads the per-model billing coefficient from the catalog and shows the real cost of every step.
OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and other families share one endpoint. Switch the fast and smart models with /models without registering anywhere else.

The generate_image action draws a picture from a prompt with AnyModel's image models and saves it into the workspace. A high-quality mode is available for the pictures that matter. With other providers the action is not offered.
On the first launch Enter opens the registration page and asks for the key. The key is checked against the catalog at once, so a wrong key fails on the spot.

install.lede: Run the release installer to install the kvist command and the Node.js needed by its terminal interface. No Python or administrator rights are needed. Choose your components and confirm installation.

steps.text: cd into the project and run kvist. The launcher uses the current directory as the workspace. The first launch asks for a provider, the models and the key, and saves them in ~/.kvist/config.json.
Type the task, or / for the command list. Approvals appear inline; answer them and the run continues. /changes shows what was written, /revert puts it back.

req: A provider API key or sign-in with a ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscription
A terminal for setup and approvals
Linux and Windows; macOS without guarantees
install.alt: Running from source requires Python 3.11+: clone the repository, install requirements.txt in a venv, and run main.py --workspace <path>. See the repository README for details.

footer.builtWith: This page ships no third-party requests, no analytics and no fonts from a CDN.
footer.release: Kvist is available to install. The source code is open under the MIT license.

meta.title: Install Kvist — step by step
meta.description: A step-by-step guide to installing Kvist on Linux, macOS and Windows: one command, the installer screen, the first-run setup, and your first task. Every screen is a real screenshot and every command can be copied.

installPage.lede: Eight steps from an empty terminal to your first task. Every screenshot is the real installer and the real interface, with the parts to look at outlined and numbered. Every command has a Copy button.
need: A terminal on Linux, macOS or Windows (macOS without guarantees)
No Python and no administrator rights are needed
A provider API key, or a ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscription to sign in with

caveat.text: They were taken from the release installer in a clean home directory. The last two show a local test gateway instead of a real provider, so the provider and model names there are not what you will see; the layout is.

steps.text: Open a terminal and paste one command. It downloads the agent and Node.js into a temporary folder and writes nothing until you confirm on the next screen.
steps.note: On Windows the installer has no component screen yet: it installs the defaults and finishes. Skip to step 07.

shots.alt: Terminal showing the installer downloading the Kvist binary and Node.js
marks: Nothing is installed until you choose it on the next screen
The agent binary downloads into a temporary folder

steps.text: Arrow keys move, Space ticks or unticks, Enter installs. The defaults are fine: the Kvist agent is required, and Node.js runs the terminal interface. Untick anything you do not want, such as the desktop app or an editor extension.

shots.alt: The installer screen listing components with checkboxes
marks: The Kvist agent: the kvist command itself
Node.js 22: runs the terminal interface
Exactly what will be written, and where
Install starts it; Esc quits with nothing written

steps.text: Each component shows its own state and the bar counts finished ones. Files go under ~/.local/share/kvist and the launcher goes to ~/.local/bin. It usually takes a minute or two.

shots.alt: The installer showing each component as working, with a progress bar
marks: One line per component you ticked
Progress and what is downloading right now

steps.text: When the installer says Installed, the same window continues into setup. It tells you what Kvist will not do: it does not read .env files or SSH keys, it asks before risky commands, and /revert undoes what it changed. Press Enter on Get started.

shots.alt: The setup welcome screen with an Installed confirmation
marks: The installation is done
The folder Kvist will work in; press F to change it
Get started continues

steps.term: Pick where the model comes from
steps.text: Choose a provider with the arrow keys or the number, then Enter. You can add more or switch later with /provider. ChatGPT Plus/Pro signs in with your subscription instead of a key; More providers opens the longer list.

shots.alt: The provider list: AnyModel, ChatGPT Plus/Pro, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and more
marks: AnyModel, Kvist's own router, is the recommended start
Sign in with a ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription
Forty more providers, set up in the classic terminal

steps.text: Paste the key and press Enter; Tab shows or hides it. It is saved only in ~/.kvist/config.json on this computer, never in a project. Without a key yet, the registration button opens the provider's page. After that the setup may ask for models and which interface to use; the first interface in the list is the one most people want.

shots.alt: The key prompt with a masked input field and a registration button
marks: Where the key is kept
Paste it here
Opens the registration page if you have no key
Continue saves it

steps.text: Go to your project folder and run kvist. The current folder becomes the workspace: Kvist reads, edits and runs commands only inside it.

shots.alt: Kvist Glass, ready for a task
marks: Where you type your request
Enter sends, Ctrl+P picks the model, Ctrl+T shows helpers
The provider, model and reasoning effort in use
The workspace: the only folder Kvist works in

steps.text: Type what you want in plain words and press Enter. Type / to see the commands. Approvals appear inline: answer them and the run continues. When it is done, /changes shows what was written and /revert puts it back.

shots.alt: A task typed into the Kvist Glass input
marks: Your request, in plain words

shots.alt: The slash command list above the input
marks: Typing / lists the commands; /commands prints them all
